title: A Large Animal Model for Pulmonary Hypertension and Right Ventricular Failure: Left Pulmonary Artery Ligation and Progressive Main Pulmonary Artery Banding in Sheep
protocol: Withhold food for 24-40 h prior to the surgical procedure to decompress the animal's rumen.
Apply a 50 μg/h fentanyl patch to a sheared area on the sheep's dorsum 12 h before the procedure.
Clean the area with chlorhexidine to remove lanolin oil residues prior to patch application.
Cover and protect the patch with an elastic tubular dressing.
Administer tiletamine/zolazepam intramuscularly (2.2-5 mg/kg) and deliver 1%-3% of isoflurane mixed with 80%-100% of oxygen via a face mask to induce anesthesia.
Position the sheep supine on the preparation table and secure its legs.
Intubate with a 10 mm endotracheal tube and start mechanical ventilation under volume-control mode (tidal volume, TV = 10 mL/kg, respiratory rate, RR = 15 breaths per minute).
Shave the surgical field from the sheep's neck to its upper abdomen.
Shave the sheep's anterior neck to expose the skin overlying the jugular veins.
Shave the anterolateral thorax bilaterally in preparation for thoracotomy.
Shave the left side of the torso from the chest to the back and caudally towards the rear flank.
Insert a 20 G angiocatheter in the auricular artery for arterial pressure monitoring and blood gas sampling.
Place a silicone tube with an inner diameter of 3/8"-1/2" for rumen decompression.
Transport the animal from the pre-operative prep room to the surgical suite.
Reconnect the sheep to the ventilator in the surgical suite.
Continue ventilation at the same setting (isoflurane 1%-3%, TV = 10 mL/kg, RR = 15 breaths per minute).
Connect the pulse oximetry sensor to the anesthetic monitor on the tongue of the animal.
Place the temperature probe into the rectum.
Connect the red lead of the electrocardiogram probe to the left rear leg.
Connect the white lead of the electrocardiogram probe to the right front leg.
Connect the black lead of the electrocardiogram probe to the left anterior leg.
Attach the male luer end of the three-way stopcock to the auricular artery angiocatheter.
Attach the female luer end of the three-way stopcock to the pressure transducer using appropriate tubing.
Align the pressure transducer at the level of the operating table.
Open the three-way stopcock on the transducer.
Select the arterial blood pressure channel on the vitals monitor.
Zero the transducer by selecting ZERO IBP.
Connect the male luer connection of the capnography monitor line to the female luer connection on the ventilator tube.
Set up IV pumps for continuous fluid and medication administration.
Perforate the septum of the saline bag with the IV administration set.
Clamp the IV tubing before perforating the bag to prevent spillage.
Fit the IV administration set tubing into the IV roller pump.
Check if the direction specified on the pump matches the direction of fluid administration.
Prime the IV line by specifying PRIME on the pump to remove air.
Position the sheep for the operative procedure.
Rotate the sheep to a partial right lateral decubitus position from the supine position.
Secure the right front foot downward and secure the left front foot while retracting it cephalad and lateral with rope or atraumatic straps.
Perform transthoracic echocardiography for baseline assessment of ventricular anatomy and function.
Determine the optimal intercostal space that facilitates surgical access to both the main pulmonary artery and the left pulmonary artery using ultrasonography.
Clean the surgical field free of dirt and other contaminants using soap or a scrub brush.
Prep the neck and chest with chlorhexidine or betadine solution.
Drape the surgical field in a sterile fashion.
Access the left or right internal jugular vein using ultrasound guidance or anatomic landmarks, finder needle, or angiocath.
Insert a 7-French triple-lumen central venous catheter into the internal jugular vein for intravenous access and central venous pressure monitoring.
Use the proximal port of the catheter for pressure monitoring.
Use the distal port of the catheter for fluid and drug administration.
Administer 20 mg/kg of cefazolin intravenously.
Administer 5 mg/kg of enrofloxacin intravenously.
Repeat dosing of cefazolin every 2-4 hours during the procedure.
Administer a 500 mL bolus of normal saline solution to augment preload before surgery.
Begin a maintenance intravenous fluid rate of 15 mL/kg/h.
Perform a muscle-sparing mini-thoracotomy at the left fourth intercostal space.
Divide the skin.
Split the pectoralis major muscle longitudinally along its fibers.
Place a self-retaining retractor to spread the muscle layer and expose the chest wall.
Divide the serratus anterior muscle.
Divide the underlying intercostal muscle in the selected intercostal space.
Enter the pleural space.
Release the intercostal muscles posteriorly toward the spine.
Release the intercostal muscles anteromedially toward the sternum.
Place self-retaining retractors to open the rib space and overlying soft tissue.
Use a small or medium Finochietto retractor to separate the ribs.
Use a Tuffier retractor within the intercostal space to improve exposure.
Incise the pericardium anterior to the phrenic nerve without injuring it.
Create a pericardial well with 2-0 silk sutures to expose the main pulmonary artery and right ventricle.
Identify the left atrial appendage within the exposure as a landmark for the level of the pulmonary artery bifurcation.
Assess the exposure and ensure that the appropriate intercostal space has been entered.
Dissect around the main pulmonary artery and isolate it with an umbilical tape.
Ensure adequate posterior dissection for eventual occluder placement and pulmonary artery flow probe.
Place a sterile flow probe into a bowl of water or saline on the sterile field to calibrate the data acquisition software.
Handoff the electrical plug on the other end to a non-sterile designee to connect the probe to the meter.
Apply a generous amount of sterile ultrasound gel in the groove of the pulmonary artery flow probe.
Fit the silicone liner into the groove of the PA flow probe.
Apply an additional layer of ultrasound gel onto the liner.
Place the PA flow probe onto the pulmonary artery (PA).
Acquire PA flow readings on the flow meter and data acquisition interface.
Check on the flow meter screen to ensure that the PA flow signal strength is 5 bars.
If the meter displays fewer than 5 bars, ensure adequate contact between the flow probe and the main PA.
Apply additional ultrasound gel if needed.
Complete intra-pericardial dissection of the left pulmonary artery (LPA).
Encircle the LPA with an umbilical tape.
Use a small sponge stick or thin malleable retractor for caudal retraction of the left atrial appendage.
Place a heavy-duty silicone vascular occluder around the main PA.
Adjust the size of the occluder based on the diameter of the pulmonary artery (PA).
Secure the ends of the vascular occluder together with a U stitch using a 0 silk suture on a Keith needle.
Slide the occluder distally along the main PA once secured.
Encircle the proximal main PA with a ½" Penrose drain.
Trim the Penrose drain to fit loosely around the PA.
Secure the Penrose to itself with a running 4-0 Prolene suture.
Establish an RV pressure line for monitoring RV pressures.
Select a location for the RV pressure line in the RV outflow tract-free wall.
Place a 5-0 monofilament, nonabsorbable polypropylene purse-string suture with pledgets surrounding the selected location.
Seat a vascular snare.
Prepare the RV pressure line by cutting off the male end of sterile 36'' pressure tubing at a 30° angle.
Use a 2-0 silk tie to mark the pressure line at an optimal depth for placement within the RV.
Make a small cardiotomy in the RVOT free wall within the previously placed purse-string suture.
Control bleeding with manual pressure or by tightening the snare on the purse-string suture.
Insert the cut end of the pressure tubing into the RV outflow tract (RVOT).
Tie down the purse-string and secure it to the pressure tubing.
Extend the RVOT tubing by connecting an additional pressure tubing to the RVOT pressure line.
Hand off the additional pressure tubing to a non-sterile designee to connect it to a pressure transducer for monitoring baseline RV pressure.
Connect IV administration set's male luer end to transducer's female luer end.
Connect pressure tubing's female luer end to transducer's male luer end.
Spike the IV administration set into a heparinized saline bag (2 IU/mL).
Fit the saline bag into a pressure bag and pump it to 250-300 mmHg as indicated on the gauge.
Fully prime the line by releasing the valve on the transducer, ensuring proper de-airing.
Dissect carefully around the LPA and encircle it with an umbilical tape.
Ligate the LPA by tying down the umbilical tape.
Increase the minute ventilation to compensate for the increased dead-space ventilation created upon LPA ligation.
Slowly inject up to 3 mL of saline into the main PA occluder.
Monitor RV pressure from the RVOT pressure line while injecting saline.
Withdraw the instilled saline once the RV response is confirmed.
Bring the RVOT pressure line and PA occluder tubing out one intercostal space below the thoracotomy incision.
Form two subdermal pockets along the fascial layer on the left dorsum of the sheep, as far posteriorly toward the spine as feasible within the sterile field.
Tunnel the RVOT pressure line and occluder tubing from the chest incision out to the left dorsum port sites using a chest tube puller.
Secure both the occluder tubing and RV pressure line to the port's barb connections.
Anchor the occluder and pressure tubing around the port connectors with additional ties.
Use the provided barbed connector fitting to protect the connection.
Seat the ports within the pre-formed subdermal pockets.
Anchor the ports in three locations around its rim to the underlying fascia with 3-0 polypropylene sutures.
Reapproximate the subcutaneous tissue, dermis, and skin in layers with polyglactin 910 sutures.
Flush the RVOT port with 5 mL of heparin sodium (1000 IU/mL).
Place a 16-French chest tube in the left pleural cavity through a separate incision.
Secure the chest tube to the skin and connect it to a closed chest tube drainage unit at a pressure of -20 cm·H2O.
Place an untied U-stitch around the chest tube.
Administer an intercostal nerve block (0.5-1 mg/kg bupivacaine) for postoperative analgesia.
Close the thoracotomy with figure-of-eight, #2 polyglactin 910 sutures.
Close the pectoralis muscle layer with running #0 polyglactin 910.
Close the subcutaneous tissue in layers of running #2-0 polyglactin 910 sutures.
Staple the skin.
Reposition the animal to dorsal recumbency, remove the orogastric tube.
Discontinue isoflurane once arterial blood pH > 7.35 and pCO2 < 55 mmHg are achieved.
Extubate the animal once it begins breathing spontaneously and lifts its head while chewing on the endotracheal tube.
Remove the chest tube prior to full anesthetic recovery.
Tie the U-stitch to close the chest tube incision.
Transfer the animal to its cage while monitoring anesthesia recovery.
Ensure supplemental oxygen (3-5 L/min by facemask) is available at all times.
Monitor vital signs every hour for the first 4 hours, every 8 hours for the next 24 hours, and once daily after that.
Monitor thoracotomy and port implantation sites daily for signs of infection.
Administer ceftiofur (5 mg/kg intramuscularly) within 24 hours after the procedure and every 3-4 days thereafter for one week.
Continue fentanyl patch postoperatively for a total of 72 hours.
Provide additional analgesia (e.g., meloxicam, 1 mg/kg once daily intramuscularly) if signs of pain persist.
Remove external sutures and skin staples 10-14 days after surgery or as recommended by veterinary staff.
Ensure port site protection from the animal rubbing or scraping against surrounding structures using a tubular dressing.
Transfer the sheep to a small enclosure.
Shear off excess wool around implanted ports.
Clean shaved areas with 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Apply topical lidocaine spray for local anesthetic.
Prepare two pressure transducers for monitoring RV and occluder cuff pressures.
Connect the female luer end of pressure tubing to the male luer end of the transducer.
Connect the male luer end of the pressure tubing to one of the female luer connections on a three-way stopcock.
Connect a 22 G Huber needle to the male luer end of that three-way stopcock.
Hang a heparinized saline bag (2 IU/mL) for RV pressure transducer.
Puncture the bag with the IV administration set for RV pressure transducer.
Connect the IV administration set's male luer connection to the female luer connection of the RV pressure transducer.
Pressurize the saline bag for RV pressure transducer.
Prime the transducer and the pressure tubing fully for occluder transducer.
Put a male luer cap on the female luer end of the pressure transducer to prevent leakage for occluder transducer.
Connect both transducers to the data acquisition hardware using an appropriate cable or adapter.
Calibrate the transducers as specified in Supplementary File 1.
Click on Start on the top right of the software window to start recording RV and PA cuff pressure waveforms at 400 Hz.
Have an assistant provide mild restraint of the animal prior to port access.
Insert Huber needle from the RV pressure transducer to the RV port.
Attach a 10 mL syringe to the three-way stopcock.
Attempt to draw blood back into the syringe from the RV port.
Inject 5-10 mL saline into the RV port to dislodge the source of occlusion if it is difficult to pull back on the syringe.
Instill 2 mg of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) into the port as a fibrinolytic agent and leave it overnight if clogging persists.
Aspirate the tPA the following day after instilling tPA.
Connect the Huber needle from the PA cuff transducer once the RV pressure line is established.
Capture the starting values of RV and PA cuff pressures.
Note any drastic changes from previous readings of RV and PA cuff pressures.
Observe the PA cuff waveform to identify leakage if the average PA cuff pressure drops at a discernible rate.
Check that all luer connections on the pressure transducer, tubing, and stopcock are tightened.
Determine the extent of leakage if the PA cuff is leaking.
Use a more frequent banding strategy if the leakage rate is slow.
Slowly inject 3% hypertonic saline into the occluder port while monitoring RV and cuff pressures.
Adjust the injection amount based on desired PH disease severity and RV phenotype.
Increase the cuff pressure by 100-150 mmHg weekly to develop an adaptive compensating RV phenotype.
Remove the Huber needle from the cuff port once the PA cuff reaches the desired inflation level.
Aspirate 10 mL of blood out of the RV port in a sterile manner and set aside.
Place a new syringe at the RV port and aspirate as much blood as needed without exceeding 7.5% of total blood volume per week.
Reconnect the original syringe with aspirated blood and return it through the RV port.
Pull on the valve lever to flush heparinized saline from the saline bag into the RV port.
Continue flushing until the line becomes clear and colorless.
Flush the RV port with 10 mL of saline.
Further flush the port with 5 mL of 1000 U/mL heparin sodium.
Repeat steps 6.1 through 6.12 every 1-4 days for 9-10 weeks.
